stem: Egg white begins to cook at 60-64°C and the yolk at 65-70°C.
explanation: So sauces with egg white cook faster than those with whole egg.

stem: A hard-fried egg is considered the easiest to digest.
explanation: The soft-boiled egg is easiest to digest.

stem: A goose egg is about twice the size of a hen egg, with an oily shell.
explanation: A goose egg is three times larger.

stem: An omelette is folded in half while the inside is still creamy, whereas a frittata is cooked on both sides.
explanation: Poached: 3 minutes in water and vinegar. Soft-boiled: 4-6 minutes from cold water.

stem: Eggs with mushrooms need a wine with persistence and quality aromas.
explanation: Mushrooms add aroma; cheese adds flavour, needing a soft wine.

stem: Boiled eggs pair with sweet, aged white wines.
explanation: Boiled eggs suit dry, young, fresh whites; the wine need not be complex unless there is sauce or spice.

stem: Olives contain about 20-25% oil and 50% water.
explanation: Plus a little sugar and about 2% other substances such as polyphenols and vitamin E.

stem: Extra virgin olive oil is mainly triglycerides of monounsaturated oleic acid.
explanation: It helps the liver and bile flow and controls cholesterol.

stem: Palm oil has a low smoke point, so it is poor for frying.
explanation: Palm oil has a high smoke point, which makes it good for frying.

stem: Butter is about 80% fat and starts to melt at 28-35°C.
explanation: 100 g gives 750 kcal and 250 mg cholesterol. Salted butter has 3-5% salt.

stem: Margarine is made by hydrogenation, which at too high a temperature produces trans fatty acids.
explanation: Hydrogen into vegetable oil at 160-180°C with a nickel or platinum catalyst. It melts at 40°C.

stem: A French person eats on average 19 kg of butter a year.
explanation: About 9 kg, and falling for health reasons.

stem: Grape vinegar needs over 6% acid and under 1.5% alcohol.
explanation: Acetobacter turns ethanol into acetic acid.

stem: Balsamic is aged in a Solera of small barrels for at least 12 years.
explanation: White grape juice is cooked at 70-80°C first to partly caramelise the sugar.

stem: Which two Italian cities are famous for balsamic vinegar?
explanation: Balsamic dishes need a soft, full-bodied, intense, persistent wine.

stem: Leek gives the most tender, rounded flavour of the onion family and is used in thick soups.
explanation: Shallots are more delicate than onions; garlic is pungent.

stem: Basil is used mainly on grilled dishes and to mask the strong smell of game.
explanation: That is rosemary. Basil is the Mediterranean leaf herb, aromatic when young.

stem: Juniper is used to remove the gamey smell of wild meat such as venison and wild rabbit.
explanation: Saffron gives yellow colour and a sweet scent.

stem: Nutmeg and clove come from Sri Lanka.
explanation: Nutmeg and clove come from the Moluccas in Indonesia; cinnamon comes from Sri Lanka.

stem: Paprika is made by blending two types of chili pepper and is used a lot in Eastern Europe.
explanation: Black pepper is pungent; pink pepper more aromatic.

stem: Star anise comes from Japan and Korea.
explanation: Star anise comes from China and Vietnam.

stem: Dry pasta is made from durum wheat and water; fresh pasta adds hen eggs.
explanation: Fresh pasta must be refrigerated and does not keep.

stem: Pizza was born in Rome in 1830.
explanation: Pizza was born in Naples (Napoli) in 1830.

stem: Which rice varieties are best for risotto?
explanation: They have the right starch for a creamy texture. Jasmine and Basmati are long-grain.

stem: Seafood added to pasta or rice increases its sweet tendency, so a fresh white balances it.
explanation: Spiced rice and curry need a wine with high aromatic stability.

stem: Tomato-sauce pasta with basil can pair with a medium-bodied, fresh white or a rosé.
explanation: Pasta with butter and parmesan suits a moderately soft, fresh, not heavy white.

stem: Asparagus is the vegetable with a sour tendency.
explanation: Tomato has the sour tendency; asparagus has sweet and bitter tendencies.

stem: Bitter vegetables need a wine with high tannin.
explanation: Bitter vegetables need a very smooth (soft) wine, red or white depending on the dish.

stem: Baked potatoes with rosemary can pair with a fragrant white such as Riesling.
explanation: They have persistence and sweet tendency.

stem: Black truffles have a sweeter aroma and a higher price than white truffles.
explanation: White truffles are sweeter-smelling and more expensive.

stem: Beans contain 30-50% starch, which gives them a sweet tendency.
explanation: Fresh beans such as winged beans also have a bitter tendency.

stem: Which group does game belong to in the meat colour system?
explanation: White: veal, rabbit, lamb, goat, chicken, turkey. Red: beef, pork, goat, horse, buffalo. Black: game.

stem: Veal and lamb are classed as red meat.
explanation: Both are white meat; red meat includes beef, pork, horse and buffalo.

stem: Meat colour comes mainly from myoglobin, a muscle pigment rich in iron.
explanation: It is also found in blood.

stem: Only female pheasant is usually eaten, as it is more fragrant.
explanation: Stewed or grilled.

stem: Foie gras on bread pairs with sweet wines such as Sauternes or Barsac.
explanation: Also Muffa Nobile. Foie gras has sweet tendency, tenderness and some bitterness.

stem: Grilled meat with charred skin calls for a soft wine with some tannin to balance its juiciness.
explanation: Fried meat calls for a fresh wine with moderate tannin.

stem: Game is paired with light, low-intensity red wines.
explanation: Game is complex and heavily seasoned: it needs a red with very high body, intensity and long aroma.

stem: Which cured meat is made from pork cheek?
explanation: Pancetta: pork belly. Bresaola: beef. Prosciutto: pork leg. Mortadella and Würstel are cooked.

stem: Bresaola is cured pork belly.
explanation: Bresaola is cured beef; pork belly is Pancetta.

stem: Fatty cured meats can pair with sparkling wine.
explanation: The bubbles cleanse the palate. Salty cured meats need a soft wine and no bitter wines.

stem: Smoked cured meat pairs best with a big, full-bodied red.
explanation: Smoked meat takes a soft red with moderate tannin; a big body should be avoided.

stem: High-fat fish has more than 10% fat; low-fat fish less than 3%.
explanation: Fillets are 18-20% protein.

stem: Crustaceans are low in fat but very high in cholesterol.
explanation: 0.5-2% fat, 80-150 mg cholesterol per 100 g.

stem: Which fish does caviar come from?
explanation: Sturgeon; Beluga, Ship, Osetra and Sevruga give differently flavoured caviar. In Russia it is paired with vodka.

stem: Belon and Marennes are famous oysters from France's Atlantic coast.
explanation: Brittany and Normandy. Oysters are rich in zinc.

stem: Oysters pair with a tannic red wine.
explanation: Oysters, with salt, oiliness and aroma, pair with a soft sparkling wine.

stem: Eel is easy to pair and suits a light still white.
explanation: Eel, salty and oily, is hard to pair but can go with a sparkling red.

stem: Fried seafood pairs with a white of high body and high alcohol.
explanation: Steamed or boiled seafood is neutral and takes a fresh, flavourful white.

stem: Pectin is the enzyme used to curdle milk for cheese.
explanation: Rennet (gastric enzyme) curdles the milk.

stem: Buffalo's milk tends to give cheese a sour taste.
explanation: Goat's milk tends to give a sour taste.

stem: Which cheese is a blue (internal mould) cheese?
explanation: Internal mould: Roquefort, Gorgonzola, Stilton, Danablu. Camembert and Brie: surface mould. Emmental: Swiss-type with eyes. Provolone: pasta filata.

stem: Mozzarella belongs to which cheese family?
explanation: With Provolone and Kashkaval.

stem: Brie and Camembert pair best with soft white wines.
explanation: Soft, short-aged cheese also suits soft Chardonnay or Sauvignon Blanc.

stem: Blue cheeses such as Gorgonzola, Roquefort and Stilton suit very full-bodied reds or soft sweet wines.
explanation: Their salinity needs softness or sweetness to balance it.

stem: Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Romano pair with a young, fresh white.
explanation: Hard, intense cheeses take a bottle-aged, evolved red with body, or a smooth sparkling wine.

stem: Match each cheese to its family.
explanation: Roquefort: internal mould. Brie: surface mould. Emmental: eyes from lactate metabolism. Feta: high salt. Parmesan: extra-hard.
